blocks.text: Overview

This week covers Thévenin and Norton equivalents for linear resistive networks, including dependent sources. Test-source analysis also handles zero open-circuit voltage. For a finite positive $R_{Th}$ and an adjustable resistive load, maximum power occurs at $R_L=R_{Th}$. Superposition then separates the contributions of independent sources.

items: Find Thévenin and Norton equivalents with the four lecture methods, and choose a method based on the kinds of sources in the network.
Convert between the Thévenin and Norton forms using $V_{Th}=v_{oc}$, $I_N=i_{sc}$ and $R_{Th}=R_N=\dfrac{v_{oc}}{i_{sc}}$.
Use a test source to find $R_{Th}$ when the network has dependent sources, including the case $V_{Th}=0$.
Derive the maximum power transfer condition $R_L=R_{Th}$ and compute $p_{\max}=\dfrac{V_{Th}^2}{4R_{Th}}$ and the resulting efficiency.
Apply superposition by turning off independent sources one at a time while keeping dependent sources active, and explain why power does not superpose.

blocks.text: Topic 1: Thévenin and Norton equivalents — four methods

A load connected to terminals $a$–$b$ cannot tell what is inside the network it is plugged into; it only sees the relationship between the terminal voltage and the terminal current. For a linear network that relationship is a straight line, and a straight line needs only two numbers. The Thévenin form stores them as a voltage source in series with a resistor, and the Norton form stores them as a current source in parallel with a resistor.
The two equivalent circuits

rows: Open-circuit voltage $v_{ab}$ with nothing connected to the terminals
Short-circuit current from $a$ to $b$ through a wire placed across the terminals
Equivalent resistance seen from the terminals, equal to $\dfrac{v_{oc}}{i_{sc}}$ when $i_{sc}\ne0$; otherwise use a test source

blocks.text: Here $v_o=v_{ab}$ and $i_o$ leaves $a$ into a load, giving $v_o=V_{Th}-R_{Th}i_o$. The relation $v_{oc}=R_{Th}i_{sc}$ holds when these quantities are finite. The ratio determines $R_{Th}$ only when $i_{sc}\ne0$: if both source responses are zero, measure the slope with a test source. Likewise, $R_{Th}=0$ needs special treatment for Norton conversion.
Choosing a method
The lecture gives four ways to get two of the three quantities. Which ones are allowed depends on whether the network contains independent sources, dependent sources, or both.

rows: Yes, when a finite unique port relation exists

blocks.text: Resistors and independent sources only: deactivate the sources and reduce (Method 2), then find whichever of $v_{oc}$ or $i_{sc}$ is easier. Dependent sources present: use $\dfrac{v_{oc}}{i_{sc}}$ (Method 1) or a test source (Methods 3 and 4). Dependent sources only: $V_{Th}=0$, so only the test-source methods give $R_{Th}$.

Deactivate independent voltage sources with shorts and independent current sources with opens. Keep dependent sources and their control relations. Plain series/parallel resistor reduction generally does not determine the resistance of a network with dependent sources; use circuit analysis with a test source.

blocks.text: Networks with dependent sources

A dependent source cannot be switched off, so the resistance has to be measured the way an instrument would measure it. Connect a test source to $a$–$b$, let the network respond, and take the ratio of terminal voltage to terminal current. If the network has no independent sources, nothing drives it when the terminals are open, so $V_{Th}=0$; the dependent source can still make $R_{Th}$ negative.

Here $v_T$ is the test-source voltage across $a$–$b$ (+ at $a$) and $i_T$ is the test current entering the network at $a$. Method 3 turns the independent sources off and uses the left formula. Method 4 keeps every source on and solves for $v_T$ as a function of $i_T$: the slope of that line is $R_{Th}$ and its intercept at $i_T=0$ is $V_{Th}$, so one analysis gives the whole equivalent.

blocks.answer: **(a)** $V_{Th}=0$. **(b)** $R_{Th}=-\tfrac{4}{3}\,\Omega\approx-1.33\,\Omega$. The resistance is negative because the dependent source supplies power.

blocks.text: When you split a circuit into a network and its load, or replace part of a circuit by its Thévenin equivalent, every dependent source must stay in the same part as the voltage or current that controls it. If the controlling variable lies in the part you replace, the equivalent no longer knows what value to give the dependent source, and the answer is wrong.
Topic 2: Maximum power transfer

Assume a finite Thévenin equivalent with $R_{Th}>0$ and an adjustable passive load $R_L\ge0$. A small load has little voltage, while a large load has little current, so load power approaches zero at both limits and has an interior maximum. The matching result below does not give a finite passive-load maximum for negative $R_{Th}$.
Deriving the condition

blocks.caption: The network replaced by its Thévenin equivalent, driving an adjustable load $R_L$.

steps.explanation: The load is in series with $R_{Th}$, so the loop current is
The power absorbed by the load is $i^2R_L$.
Differentiate with respect to $R_L$ (quotient rule); $V_{Th}$ and $R_{Th}$ are fixed by the network.

The derivative is zero only when the numerator vanishes. It is positive below this value and negative above it, so this is a maximum. This assumes $R_{Th}>0$ and $V_{Th}\ne0$; when $V_{Th}=0$ the power is zero for every nonsingular passive load.
Substitute $R_L=R_{Th}$ back into $p_L$.

blocks.text: For $R_{Th}>0$, the matched adjustable load is $R_L=R_{Th}$ and receives $p_{\max}=\dfrac{V_{Th}^2}{4R_{Th}}$. The Norton expression uses $V_{Th}=R_{Th}I_N$. Half the Thévenin voltage appears across the matched load. These statements require a finite equivalent and a positive resistance.
Using the result

Maximum power transfer is not maximum efficiency. At $R_L=R_{Th}$ the Thévenin resistance dissipates as much as the load, and the real sources inside the network may waste even more. Also, the condition assumes the load is the adjustable element: if instead a resistor in series with a fixed load is adjustable, as in Textbook P4.84, the load power is largest when that series resistance is zero.

blocks.title: Lecture example · Maximum power is not maximum efficiency

blocks.text: For maximum power problems, always find the Thévenin equivalent first, using whichever Topic 1 method fits the sources. Then go back to the original circuit for anything about the internal sources (power supplied, efficiency), because the equivalent only describes behaviour at the terminals.
Topic 3: Superposition

In these linear resistive circuits, each output voltage or current is a weighted sum of independent source values, with weights set by the resistances and dependent-source gains. Turn off the other independent sources and sum the signed contributions. Superposition also applies to linear dynamic circuits, but nonzero initial stored energy contributes a natural response that must be included once, not duplicated in every source contribution.
The principle

Here $y$ is any branch voltage or current in the full circuit, $n$ is the number of independent sources, and $y_k$ is the value of that same variable when only independent source $k$ is on. Keep the reference direction of $y$ the same in every sub-circuit, so that the signs add correctly.

rows: Its value is set by a variable in the sub-circuit

The $2\,\Omega$ branch carries half of the $12\,\mathrm{A}$, and $v''_1$ follows from a divider on the $4\,\Omega$ branch.

blocks.title: Lecture example · Superposition with two independent sources

blocks.text: Dependent sources and power

Dependent sources are part of the circuit's linear "machinery", not inputs, so they stay on in every sub-circuit and simply react to whatever the remaining independent source produces. Power, however, is a product of a voltage and a current, so it is not linear in the sources.

```schematic
R1 0,3 -> 3,3 "$5\,\Omega$" i="$i_\Delta$"
R2 3,3 -> 3,0 "$20\,\Omega$" v="$v_o$"
G1 6,3 -> 3,3 "$\alpha v_\Delta$"
R3 6,3 -> 6,0 "$10\,\Omega$" v="$v_\Delta$"
E1 6,0 -> 3,0 "$\beta i_\Delta$"
I1 9,0 -> 9,3 "$5\,\mathrm{A}$"
wire 6,3 -> 9,3
wire 6,0 -> 9,0
wire 0,0 -> 3,0
label 3,3 "a" above
label 6,3 "d" above
label 6,0 "c" below
ground 3,0
```

- $V_{S1}=10\,\mathrm{V}$, $I_{S3}=5\,\mathrm{A}$
- $I_{S2}=\alpha v_\Delta$ with $\alpha=0.4\,\mathrm{A/V}$
- $V_{S4}=\beta i_\Delta$ with $\beta=2\,\Omega$

1. Find $v'_o$ with only $V_{S1}$ on.
2. Find $v''_o$ with only $I_{S3}$ on.
3. Find $v_o$.

steps.explanation: $V_{S1}$ alone: open $I_{S3}$. KCL at $d$: the only currents leaving $d$ are $\alpha v_\Delta$ (to $a$) and $\dfrac{v_\Delta}{10}$ (down $R_3$), and nothing enters.

The right-hand resistor and dependent current source carry zero current because $v_\Delta=0$. The left $5\,\Omega$ and $20\,\Omega$ resistors form a divider. The controlling current is still $i_\Delta=\dfrac{10-8}{5}=0.4\,\mathrm{A}$, so the dependent voltage source remains at $0.8\,\mathrm{V}$; it does not change this divider.
$I_{S3}$ alone: short $V_{S1}$. KCL at $d$: $5\,\mathrm{A}$ enters from $I_{S3}$ and leaves through the dependent source and $R_3$.

The $4\,\mathrm{A}$ enters node $a$, which now sees $5\,\Omega$ (to the shorted source) in parallel with $20\,\Omega$. The voltage source $\beta i_\Delta$ only sets $v_c$ and does not change this KCL.
Add the contributions.

blocks.title: Lecture example · Superposition with dependent sources

blocks.text: Here $v'$, $i'$ are an element's voltage and current from the first source alone, $v''$, $i''$ are from the second source alone, and $p'=v'i'$, $p''=v''i''$ are the powers in each sub-circuit. The cross terms are generally non-zero, so the true power is not the sum of the sub-circuit powers. Find the total $v$ and $i$ by superposition first, then compute $p=vi$.

Two common superposition mistakes: (1) turning off a dependent source — only independent sources are switched off; (2) adding powers from the sub-circuits. For example, in the two-source lecture example the $4\,\Omega$ resistor absorbs $\dfrac{20^2}{4}=100\,\mathrm{W}$ and $\dfrac{(-24)^2}{4}=144\,\mathrm{W}$ in the two sub-circuits, but only $\dfrac{(-4)^2}{4}=4\,\mathrm{W}$ in the real circuit.

Superposition pays off when each one-source sub-circuit collapses to dividers and series/parallel reductions, or when you need to know how much each source contributes. If the circuit has many sources or tangled dependent sources, a single nodal or mesh analysis is usually faster.
Practice problems

Try each problem before opening the solution. The first two need only Thévenin basics, the middle ones practise superposition and dependent sources, and the last combines a dependent source with maximum power transfer. For each Thévenin problem, decide which of the four methods you will use before writing any equations.

steps.explanation: $45\,\mathrm{V}$ alone (short $10\,\mathrm{V}$, open $8\,\mathrm{A}$): $10+30=40\,\Omega$ is in parallel with $40\,\Omega$, in series with $5\,\Omega$ and $15\,\Omega$.

$10\,\mathrm{V}$ alone (short $45\,\mathrm{V}$, open $8\,\mathrm{A}$): the source sees $10+\big(40\parallel(5+15)\big)+30=53.33\,\Omega$. The part of its current that goes through $5\,\Omega$ flows down through the shorted $45\,\mathrm{V}$ position, against $i_o$.

$8\,\mathrm{A}$ alone (both voltage sources shorted): the bridge is balanced because $\dfrac{10}{5}=\dfrac{30}{15}$, so the $40\,\Omega$ carries no current. The $8\,\mathrm{A}$ splits between the $10+5=15\,\Omega$ and $30+15=45\,\Omega$ paths.
Add the contributions (a DC simulation of the full circuit confirms $7\,\mathrm{A}$).

blocks.title: Textbook P4.93 · Superposition with a hidden balanced bridge

blocks.prompt:
The variable resistor $R_o$ is adjusted for maximum power transfer. The dependent source $v_\phi$ equals the voltage across the $4\,\Omega$ resistor in series with the $20\,\mathrm{V}$ source.

```schematic
V1 0,4 -> 0,0 "$100\,\mathrm{V}$"
R1 0,4 -> 3,4 "$4\,\Omega$"
R2 3,4 -> 6,4 "$4\,\Omega$"
R3 3,4 -> 3,2 "$4\,\Omega$" v="$v_\phi$"
V2 3,2 -> 3,0 "$20\,\mathrm{V}$"
wire 0,4 -> 0,7
E1 3,7 -> 0,7 "$v_\phi$"
R4 3,7 -> 6,7 "$4\,\Omega$"
wire 6,7 -> 6,4
wire 6,4 -> 8,4
R5 8,4 -> 8,0 "$R_o$"
wire 0,0 -> 8,0
label 8,4 "a" above
ground 0,0
```

1. Find the value of $R_o$ for maximum power transfer.
2. Find the maximum power delivered to $R_o$.

steps.explanation: The dependent source rules out deactivation, so use $v_{oc}$ and $i_{sc}$. Call the centre node $v_1$; then $v_\phi=v_1-20$ and the top node is at $100+v_\phi=80+v_1$. Open circuit, KCL at $a$: the two $4\,\Omega$ currents into $a$ cancel.
KCL at the centre node, then substitute $v_a$.
Short circuit ($v_a=0$): KCL at the centre node gives $v_1$, then add the two currents into the short.
Thévenin resistance and the matched load.
Maximum power.

blocks.title: Assessment AP 4.21 · Maximum power with a dependent source

blocks.text: Summary

items: A linear resistive port with finite equivalents has $V_{Th}=v_{oc}$ and $I_N=i_{sc}$. Use $R_{Th}=\dfrac{v_{oc}}{i_{sc}}$ when $i_{sc}\ne0$; use a test source if both are zero.
Deactivating sources (voltage source → short, current source → open) gives $R_{Th}$ only when the network has no dependent sources.
With dependent sources, use $\dfrac{v_{oc}}{i_{sc}}$ or a test source. A network with only dependent sources has $V_{Th}=0$, and its $R_{Th}=\dfrac{v_T}{i_T}$ can be negative.
Method 4 needs one analysis: with all sources on, $v_T=R_{Th}\,i_T+V_{Th}$.
A dependent source must stay in the same part of the circuit as its controlling variable when you split or replace parts of a circuit.

A load receives maximum power when $R_L=R_{Th}$, and then $p_{\max}=\dfrac{V_{Th}^2}{4R_{Th}}$. That is not maximum efficiency (only $35.7\%$ in the lecture example). The matching result assumes finite $R_{Th}>0$ and an adjustable passive load.
Superposition: switch off one independent source at a time, never a dependent source, and add voltages and currents — never powers.
